blocks.html: This point also gave great argument for thinking that there was trickery got up against the accused, and that what the said de Rols did was by the constraint, force and reverence of the said Pierre Guerre and her mother, in whose house she lived: for although one ought not easily to presume an act to have been done through terror or fear a2, nevertheless, when such solicitations, importunities and threats appear, the fear is sufficiently proved b; considering especially the quality of those who used such intimidations, who were the stepfather and the mother c; and considering the place also, for it was in their house, where the said de Rols was maintained, and held in captivity d; and considering moreover her own quality, who was a woman, who is frightened and terrified at a small thing e, and moreover lets herself easily be persuaded — and in her, persuasions have no less force than threats or force f. Added to which also, she daily made complaint of it against her said stepfather and mother g.

notes.citation: Digest 17.2.51 (Pro socio, l. Merito; cited at annot-037 {b} for the rule that fraud is not presumed); Digest 50.17 (De diversis regulis iuris antiqui), l. Quoties, § Qui dolo (fragment and paragraph not identified)
notes.original: l. merito. D pro ſoc. l. quo ries. P. qui do lo D. de regu. iur.
notes.gloss: Fear, like fraud, is not presumed but must be proved.

notes.citation: Innocent IV on Decretals X 2.24.31 (De iureiurando, c. Petitio; Honorius III, on an oath extorted by a prince who feared conspiracies)
notes.original: Innocent au c. petitio. de iure iu.
notes.gloss: On when fear is held to be sufficiently proved.

notes.citation: Digest 44.5.1.5 (Quarum rerum actio non datur, l. [1], § Quae onerandae; Ulpian, on the obligations a patron imposes on his freedman; the law's incipit is lost in the print, which reads l...)
notes.original: l... P. quæ onerandæ. D. quar. rer.
notes.gloss: Cited for the standing of the person who exacts the act — the patron over the freedman, as here the stepfather and mother over the daughter. The transcription runs this note and the next together as one note keyed c.

notes.citation: Digest 4.2 (Quod metus causa gestum erit), l. Qui in carcerem (cf. D. 4.2.22, Paul: what is done by one who has been shut up in prison to extort something from him is of no effect; the print's car. cerẽ is carcerem with a reflow gap, the qui in being lost or run into the preceding note)
notes.original: car. cerẽ D. quod met. cau.

notes.citation: The Gloss and the Doctors on Decretals X 4.1 (De sponsalibus et matrimoniis), c. Cum locum (X 4.1.14)
notes.original: La gloſe & les Docteurs. au c. cum locũ de ſponſa.
notes.gloss: Consent has no place where fear or coercion intervenes; the commentators there discuss the fear that can move a steadfast woman.

notes.citation: Digest, a title printed de in ius. (perhaps De in ius vocando, D. 2.4), l. 1, § Usque adeo — not identified; Code 9.13 (De raptu virginum, seu viduarum, nec non sanctimonialium), the sole law (C. 9.13.1, Justinian), at the words Volentibus
notes.original: l j. P. vſque adeo. D. de in ius. l. vnique. en ces paroles, Volẽtibus. C. de rap. virgi.
notes.gloss: Justinian punishes the ravisher even where the women were willing, the will of a woman being easily bent — Coras's point that persuasion works upon a woman as force does. The print's vnique is vnica, the sole law.

notes.citation: Digest 29.2.6.7 (De adquirenda vel omittenda hereditate, l. Qui in aliena, the last paragraph; Ulpian, citing Celsus: one who enters on an inheritance under compulsion of fear does not become heir), and the Interpreters there
notes.original: l. qui in aliena. P. fin. D. de aquir. hære. & les Interpretes.
notes.gloss: The bearing of the fragment on complaint as proof of compulsion could not be verified.
